It notes regulatory and other operating risks, directs readers to relevant report sections, and explains where company filings, governance materials, and SEC information are available online.

nodes.title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS
Supply and Demand
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s results face risks from commodity price and margin volatility, affecting Upstream when prices fall and downstream segments when they rise. Lower-emission ventures depend on market growth, supportive policy, and commercially viable technology. Demand risks include recessions, demographic and political change, trade disruption, security and public-health events, financial-market distress, alternative energy and efficiency advances, weather, and changing consumer preferences. Supply risks include new production and capacity, OPEC+ quotas, emissions policies, conflict, disasters, competitor disruptions, logistics, and technology. Interest rates, inflation, currencies, dollar use, regional conditions, and hedging or trading losses also pose risks.

nodes.title: Government and Political Factors
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s operations and results face political, regulatory, legal, and security risks: limits on resource access, investment, trade, and business imposed by governments or sanctions; uncertain legal systems and contract enforcement; changing laws, policies, taxes, royalties, price controls, environmental and operational rules, permits, disclosure and technology requirements, and government actions such as contract cancellation or expropriation; litigation and enforcement, including punitive damages and policy-driven lawsuits; and unrest, sabotage, terrorism, cyberattacks, or national-security restrictions that can raise costs or disrupt operations.

nodes.title: Climate Change and the Energy Transition
nodes.summary: The text outlines climate-related transition risks and opportunities: net-zero goals rely on uncertain scenarios, technologies, policies, and markets, requiring ExxonMobil to identify energy-system shifts and invest strategically. Emissions policies and pressure on oil-and-gas financing may raise costs, delay projects, weaken returns and demand, and increase compliance burdens. Lower-emission technologies—including CCS, hydrogen, fuels, lithium, and efficiency—are pursued through research and partnerships, but commercial success depends on innovation and cost competitiveness. LCS investments also depend on durable government support and market development; restrictive policies without matching demand reductions could cause price volatility, inflation, shortages, and economic or policy disruption.

nodes.title: Operational and Other Factors
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s results depend on controllable operational factors, capital allocation, and co-venturer performance. Risks include exploration and development success; management of major projects and the overall portfolio, including partner negotiations, costs, markets, technical issues, asset sales, and retained liabilities; operational efficiency and acquisition integration; technology, R&D, and adapting to new technologies; safety, environmental protection, business controls, and enterprise risk management; cybersecurity threats affecting the company and third parties; preparedness for severe weather and other disruptions; limited insurance availability and affordability; intense competition from private and state-owned firms, service companies, and alternative energy; and reputational harm. Forward-looking plans and estimates may differ materially from actual outcomes.

ExxonMobil faces risks from commodity prices, demand and supply shifts, economic and financial conditions, and uncertainty in lower-emission markets. Government, legal, political, security, and climate-transition developments may restrict operations, increase costs, disrupt projects, or affect demand and returns. Operational risks include exploration, project and portfolio management, partners, technology, safety, environmental and cybersecurity controls, severe disruptions, insurance, competition, and reputation. Plans and estimates may not match actual results.

title: ITEM 1C. CYBERSECURITY
summary: The Corporation integrates cybersecurity into enterprise risk management, with Audit Committee oversight and annual program review. Its VP of IT and experienced IT/OT cybersecurity operations managers lead daily prevention, detection, investigation, and response, reporting on strategy, metrics, testing, preparedness, and threats to senior management and the Board or Audit Committee. The program uses layered technology, NIST frameworks, incident-response plans, annual training and drills, external expert testing, threat sharing, and risk-based third-party screening. No known threats or prior incidents have materially affected or are likely to materially affect the Corporation, but protections cannot eliminate all risk; further risks are discussed in Item 1A.

nodes.title: Canada / Other Americas
nodes.summary: The text outlines petroleum license and contract terms in Canada, Argentina, Brazil, and Guyana. In Canada, onshore leases vary in length and may be renewed or retained through work and proven production; offshore exploration depends on work commitments and rentals, production licenses last 25 years with extensions, and significant-discovery licenses have no fixed term. Argentina sets production terms of 35 years for unconventional and 25 years for conventional onshore concessions, with unlimited 10-year extensions; offshore licenses granted in 2019 last eight years in two four-year periods, with optional five-year extensions. Brazilian concessions allow up to eight years for exploration and 27 for production; PSCs allow up to seven and 28 years, respectively. Guyana’s 2023 Act permits petroleum agreements, typically with exploration periods up to 10 years, and production periods of 20 years for oil or 30 for gas, each renewable for up to 10 years.

nodes.title: Europe
nodes.summary: The text outlines European oil and gas license terms. Germany grants exploration concessions for up to five years, extendable repeatedly by up to three years with work commitments; historical production licenses lasted 20–25 years and could be extended while producing. In the Netherlands, licenses issued since 2003 last as specified according to required activities, while older production rights retain varied onshore and offshore terms. UK acreage terms vary by government policy: early licenses had six-year initial terms, relinquishment, and possible long extensions; most traditional licenses now have four-year exploration and extension periods, followed by an 18-year production term, with required acreage relinquishments.

nodes.title: Africa
nodes.summary: The text outlines petroleum contract and license regimes in four African countries. Angola uses production-sharing agreements or other contracts, with 3–4-year exploration terms, extension options, and 20–30-year production periods. Equatorial Guinea uses state-negotiated production-sharing contracts with 30-year crude production terms; ExxonMobil is pursuing an exit. Mozambique generally uses government concession contracts: Area 4’s EPCC lasts 30 years from an approved development plan, while Area 5 interests were progressively relinquished, with remaining acreage relinquished in 2023. Nigeria’s deepwater operations use NNPCL-backed PSCs, generally lasting 30 years; shallow-water pre-1969 leases, renewed for 20 years in 2011, operate through NNPCL joint ventures under Petroleum Profits Tax Act terms. The 2021 Petroleum Industry Act governs future renewals.

nodes.title: Asia
nodes.summary: The text outlines ExxonMobil’s Asian oil and gas agreements and their terms: Azerbaijan’s Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli PSA runs to 2049 after a 2017 extension; Indonesian PSCs generally allow six years of exploration, one four-year extension, a 30-year total term, and government-approved extensions of up to 20 years; Iraq’s West Qurna Phase I contract provided 20 years plus a possible five-to-15-year extension and cost recovery with production fees, but ExxonMobil exited in 2024. Kazakhstan’s onshore production period is 40 years from 1993, while offshore terms include exploration, appraisal, 20-year production periods, and possible two 10-year extensions. Malaysian PSCs generally run 25 years, subject to approval for extensions. Qatar gas project rights generally run 25 years, with terms and extensions requiring state approval. Thailand concessions allow 30 years plus a 10-year extension. UAE Upper Zakum agreements were extended to 2051.

nodes.title: Australia / Oceania
nodes.summary: Australia’s offshore petroleum activities in Commonwealth waters are federally regulated. Exploration permits run six years, with two possible five-year renewals; retention leases cover resources expected to become viable within 15 years, last five years, and may be renewed. Production licenses issued before July 1998 had a 21-year term, one 21-year renewal, then indefinite duration; newer licenses are indefinite. Either may terminate after five years without production. In Papua New Guinea, the Oil and Gas Act governs activities: prospecting licenses run six years, with a possible five-year extension (and, in certain cases, another three years), generally requiring 50% area relinquishment; development licenses run 25 years, with discretionary extensions of up to 20 years each. Retention licenses for gas expected to become viable within 15 years run five years and may, at ministerial discretion, be extended twice, up to 15 years total.

Capital employed is presented from both business asset-and-liability and corporate debt-and-equity perspectives, including equity-company amounts, with figures for 2021–2023. ExxonMobil considers ROCE a useful historical capital-productivity measure, while using cash-flow-based measures for investment decisions. A 2021–2023 table reports earnings and financing-cost components, earnings excluding financing costs, average capital employed, and corporate ROCE of 10.9%, 24.9%, and 15.0%, respectively.

nodes.title: OVERVIEW
nodes.summary: Management is responsible for ExxonMobil’s financial analysis and statements, which reflect its integrated operations across oil and gas, products, and lower-emission opportunities. The company reports Upstream, Energy Products, Chemical Products, and Specialty Products, with voluntary geographic detail, and is organized into Upstream, Product Solutions, and Low Carbon Solutions; centralized service groups support these businesses. Its resources, finances, technology, disciplined investment, and integrated model support reliable, affordable lower-emission energy development and help mitigate commodity-price risk. Annual Outlook and Corporate Plan processes set economic assumptions and operating and capital goals, including prices, margins, volumes, costs, emissions pricing, and exchange rates. Investments are tested across market conditions, based on updated field profiles, and reappraised so lessons inform future projects.

nodes.title: BUSINESS ENVIRONMENT
Long-Term Business Outlook
Developing countries projected to drive energy demand growth
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s 2023 Outlook, based on long-term market fundamentals and scenarios including IPCC and IEA pathways, informs planning while recognizing uncertainty and monitoring transition signposts. It projects population and economic growth will raise global energy demand nearly 15% by 2050, mainly in developing countries, while efficiency lowers energy and emissions per economic output. Electricity demand rises 80%, with renewables, gas, and nuclear replacing much coal. Transportation energy grows over 30%; electric vehicles and efficiency reduce light-duty liquid-fuel use, while commercial fleets largely retain liquid fuels. Industry and buildings also need more energy. Liquid-fuel demand rises about 15%, with non-OECD markets expanding and diverse supply sources needed. Natural gas grows nearly 25%, led by Asia Pacific, supplied by conventional and unconventional gas and expanding LNG trade.

nodes.title: Oil and natural gas projected to play a critical role in the global energy mix
nodes.summary: The text presents ExxonMobil’s 2023 outlook for a diverse global energy mix through 2050: oil remains near 30% and the largest source; natural gas rises above 25%, coal declines to about half its share, nuclear grows, renewables exceed 20%, and wind and solar grow more than fivefold from 2021 to roughly 10%. It also describes lower-carbon technologies and policies needed to decarbonize industry and transport, including lower-emission fuels, hydrogen and ammonia, electrification, and carbon capture and storage for hard-to-abate sectors.

nodes.title: Significant oil and natural gas investment needed to meet projected global demand
nodes.summary: The section discusses projected global oil and gas supply and demand, citing IEA, ExxonMobil, and IPCC scenarios, and says significant investment and technology are needed through 2050—even under rapid-demand-decline scenarios. ExxonMobil’s Outlook assumes resource growth from discoveries and existing fields, increasingly stringent climate policies, and successful national Paris Agreement commitments despite UNEP’s warning that G20 nations may fall short. It models CO₂ costs reaching up to $150 per metric ton in OECD and $100 in non-OECD nations by 2050, notes policy uncertainty and affordability and reliability needs, and monitors COP 28 commitments. Outlook estimates draw on internal analyses and public sources.

ExxonMobil’s 2023 Outlook uses long-term market fundamentals and external scenarios to guide planning while recognizing uncertainty and monitoring transition policies and signposts. It projects energy demand to grow nearly 15% by 2050, mainly in developing countries, alongside efficiency gains and changing fuel use across electricity, transport, industry and buildings. Oil remains the largest energy source, gas grows, coal declines, and renewables and nuclear expand; decarbonization requires technologies such as electrification, lower-emission fuels, hydrogen, ammonia and carbon capture. Meeting projected oil and gas demand requires substantial investment and technology even in rapid-transition scenarios, amid uncertain climate policies, affordability and reliability needs, and possible gaps in national commitments.

nodes.title: Progress Reducing Emissions
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil describes its strategy for creating shareholder value while contributing to the energy transition. It aims for net-zero Scope 1 and 2 emissions from operated assets by 2050, with a 2030 net-zero target for operated Permian assets; detailed roadmaps are updated as technology and policy evolve. Relative to 2016, 2030 targets include reductions of 20–30% in corporate greenhouse-gas intensity, 70–80% in methane intensity, 40–50% in upstream greenhouse-gas intensity, and 60–70% in flaring intensity, plus about a 20% absolute emissions reduction. Plans cover operated assets and exclude Denbury. The company is pursuing lower-emission investments in carbon capture and storage, hydrogen, lower-emission fuels, and lithium, emphasizing the need for supportive policy, technology advances, and market mechanisms. Denbury’s acquisition adds more than 900 miles of CO₂ pipelines, supporting Gulf Coast carbon capture and storage for ExxonMobil and industrial customers.

nodes.title: Energy Markets, Kazakhstan Transport, and European Taxes
key_items: Additional European Taxes on the Energy Sector
nodes.summary: The page reviews energy-market conditions: post-pandemic underinvestment and supply constraints lifted prices and refining margins through 2022, while markets and inflation moderated in 2023; chemical margins stayed weak. The Corporation reports $9.7 billion in structural savings since 2019 and identifies further efficiency opportunities. It outlines risks to Kazakhstan oil exports via CPC amid regional conflict, noting 2023 earnings and production exposure. It also describes the EU’s 2022–23 surplus-profits tax, related charges, and expected remaining payments.

The section covers ExxonMobil’s long-term energy outlook, including projected demand, changing fuel mix, decarbonization needs, investment requirements and uncertainties around policy, affordability and reliability. It describes emissions-reduction targets and plans for operated assets, investments in lower-emission technologies, and Denbury’s CO₂ pipeline contribution. It also reviews energy-market conditions, structural cost savings, risks to Kazakhstan oil exports through the CPC, and European surplus-profits taxes and expected payments.

nodes.title: BUSINESS RESULTS
Upstream
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil outlines its Upstream strategy: prioritize low-cost, accretive resources, technology, efficiency, emissions reduction, and operational excellence, with expected growth in Americas, unconventional, deepwater, and LNG production. It reports Guyana discoveries and FPSO ramp-up, Permian growth and emissions initiatives, the proposed Pioneer acquisition, and progress on LNG projects. Tables present 2021–2023 regional production and earnings; analyses attribute earnings changes to prices, volumes/mix, other factors, and identified items. Production reconciliations explain year-over-year trends and define entitlement, government-mandate, divestment, and growth factors, alongside market and operational uncertainties.

nodes.title: Energy Products
key_items: Energy Products Operational Results; Refinery throughput; Worldwide
nodes.summary: Describes Energy Products’ integrated fuels business and how refining margins, operations, product mix, and cost control affect earnings, including 2023 margin trends and volatility factors. Lists recent capacity projects and asset divestments/sales. Reports 2021–2023 segment earnings, identified items and adjusted earnings; explains 2023 and 2022 earnings drivers, including margins, volume/mix, other factors, and identified items. Provides 2021–2023 refinery throughput and energy-product sales by region and product category, with accounting notes.

nodes.title: Chemical Products
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s Chemical Products segment makes olefins, polyolefins and intermediates, leveraging scale, integration, technology, operational excellence and cost discipline; long-term chemical demand is expected to outpace economic growth. In 2023, bottom-of-cycle margins reflected excess capacity, while feed and energy advantages, reliability and performance-product sales supported results. Baytown started 400,000-tonne performance polymers and 350,000-tonne linear alpha olefins units; a China complex planned to add over 2.5 million tonnes annually. Earnings were $1.637 billion in 2023, $3.543 billion in 2022 and $6.989 billion in 2021; 2023 identified-item losses were $388 million, mainly impairments. Lower margins, unfavorable mix and higher expenses reduced 2023 earnings; margins, mix, expenses and currency effects reduced 2022 earnings. Worldwide sales were 19.382 million tonnes in 2023, 19.167 million in 2022 and 19.142 million in 2021.

nodes.title: Specialty Products
key_items: Specialty Products Operational Results; Specialty Products sales (2)
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil Specialty Products makes and markets performance products, including lubricants, basestocks, waxes, synthetics, elastomers, and resins, using proprietary technology and brands to serve transportation and industrial customers. In 2023, earnings were $2.714 billion ($2.807 billion excluding identified items), with stronger margins offset partly by lower volumes; other effects were positive, and identified losses mainly reflected impairments. The Singapore Resid Upgrade project advanced toward a 2025 start-up. The text also reports 2022 and 2021 earnings, identified items and earnings factors, and 2021–2023 U.S., non-U.S., and worldwide sales volumes.

nodes.title: Corporate and Financing
Corporate and Financing Financial Results
nodes.summary: Corporate and Financing supports operating segments through administration, financing and insurance; Low Carbon Solutions remains there until substantial assets and contracts are established. The 2023 Denbury acquisition expanded carbon-capture and enhanced-oil-recovery capabilities. Segment losses were $1.791 billion in 2023, $1.663 billion in 2022 and $2.636 billion in 2021; changes reflected tax, pension and financing-cost effects. Cash flow tables show operating, investing and financing activity and year-end cash. Cash rose $1.9 billion to $31.6 billion in 2023, versus a $22.9 billion increase to $29.7 billion in 2022; sources and uses included earnings, depreciation, asset-sale proceeds, capital spending, dividends, share repurchases, investments, working capital and debt reduction. ExxonMobil expects internal funds, supplemented by debt, to meet requirements; it had $0.3 billion of undrawn short-term and $1.3 billion of long-term credit lines. The discussion describes field-decline and production uncertainties, oil and gas price dependence, projects and portfolio diversity as risk mitigants, and 2023 capital and exploration spending of $26.3 billion, with $23–25 billion planned for 2024. It also covers continuing asset sales and acquisitions and their evaluation criteria and financing. Operating cash flow was $55.4 billion in 2023, down $21.4 billion, and $76.8 billion in 2022, up $28.7 billion, with earnings, depreciation, asset-sale gains, equity-company dividends and working capital as drivers. Investing cash use was $19.3 billion in 2023 and $14.7 billion in 2022, reflecting changes in capital spending, asset-sale proceeds, investments and other receipts.

nodes.title: Asset Management and Cash Flow Results
nodes.summary: The Corporation discusses ongoing asset upgrades and occasional asset dispositions, which may generate gains or losses, and acquisitions evaluated for strategic fit, synergies, growth, supply costs, and valuation, funded with cash, shares, or both. Operating cash flow was $55.4 billion in 2023, down $21.4 billion, and $76.8 billion in 2022, up $28.7 billion, with changes in net income, depreciation, asset-sale gains, equity-company dividends, and working capital. Investing activities used $19.3 billion in 2023 and $14.7 billion in 2022; the text compares capital spending, asset-sale and investment-return proceeds, additional investments, advances, and other investing proceeds with prior years.

nodes.title: Financing Cash Flow, Obligations, and Guarantees
nodes.summary: Financing cash use was $34.3 billion in 2023, down from $39.1 billion in 2022; dividends totaled $14.9 billion each year, and share repurchases continued under a program of up to $50 billion through 2024. The company anticipated repurchases of $20 billion annually through 2025 after the Pioneer transaction, subject to market conditions; in 2022 it also reduced debt by $7.2 billion. Contractual obligations include leases, debt, retirement and benefit obligations, and purchase and capital commitments. Commodity purchases are offset by related sales; take-or-pay and unconditional purchase obligations totaled $44.3 billion at year-end 2023, with $4.1 billion and $4.3 billion due in 2024 and 2025. Guarantees cover debt and contractual performance; estimated exposures are described, and they are not expected to materially affect financial results or resources.

nodes.title: Financial Strength and Contingencies
nodes.summary: At year-end 2023, the Corporation had $0.3 billion in unused short-term and $1.3 billion in unused long-term committed credit lines. Debt-to-capital ratios are reported for 2021–2023. Management considers financial strength a strategic advantage that supports access to capital markets and major long-term commitments. Debt fell $6.5 billion in 2022, returning to pre-pandemic levels, and remained relatively flat in 2023 at $41.6 billion. ExxonMobil and subsidiaries face pending lawsuits, but the Corporation does not expect their outcomes to materially affect operations, financial condition, or statements; no other unreported events or uncertainties indicate material future changes. See Note 16 for details.

Covers Corporate and Financing’s role, Low Carbon Solutions’ placement, and Denbury’s acquisition; segment losses and their drivers; cash flows, cash balances, capital plans, funding sources, and liquidity; operating and investing activity; asset upgrades, sales, and acquisitions; dividends, repurchases, and debt; contractual obligations and guarantees; financial strength, leverage, and access to capital; and pending litigation and other contingencies.

Reports results and strategies for Upstream, Energy Products, Chemical Products, Specialty Products, and Corporate and Financing. Covers segment operations, growth projects, acquisitions and divestments, market and operating conditions, emissions initiatives, earnings and identified items, earnings drivers, production, throughput and sales volumes, and related definitions and accounting notes. Also discusses cash flows, liquidity, capital plans and funding, investment and asset transactions, shareholder distributions, debt, contractual obligations, guarantees, financial strength, litigation, and contingencies.

nodes.title: CAPITAL AND EXPLORATION EXPENDITURES
nodes.summary: Defines Capex as before-tax additions to property, plant and equipment plus exploration expenses, including equity-company shares but excluding specified noncash acquisitions and exploration-support depreciation; management focuses on controllable spending. Tables compare U.S., non-U.S., and total spending by business for 2023 and 2022. Capex was $26.3 billion in 2023; planned 2024 investment is $23–25 billion, including $10.5 billion of firm commitments, with another $9.2 billion committed for 2025 onward; actual spending may vary. Upstream spending rose 16% to $19.8 billion, driven by the Permian and Guyana. Projects take years to produce; developed reserves were 63% of proved reserves, above 60% for a decade. Product Solutions invested $5.9 billion, up $0.3 billion, including projects in China and Singapore. Other spending of $0.6 billion mainly supported carbon capture and storage, lithium, and hydrogen.

nodes.title: TAXES
nodes.summary: The text reports ExxonMobil’s taxes and environmental matters. Total income-statement taxes fell to $47.6 billion in 2023 from $51.6 billion in 2022, while income tax expense declined to $15.4 billion from $20.2 billion; the effective rate remained 33%, and other taxes and duties rose to $32.2 billion. In 2022, total taxes rose from $40.6 billion in 2021, with income tax expense increasing, the effective rate reaching 33% from 31%, and other taxes and duties declining. Environmental expenditures were $7.1 billion in 2023, including $4.3 billion in expenses; spending is forecast at $9.7 billion in 2024 and $10.2 billion in 2025, with projected capital shares of 47% and 51%. The company describes prevention and remediation efforts and its policy for accruing probable, estimable environmental liabilities, including at multi-party sites. No individual site is expected to cause material losses. 2023 provisions were $208 million, and year-end liabilities were $701 million, versus $185 million and $730 million in 2022.

nodes.title: MARKET RISKS
nodes.summary: The text reports 2021–2023 worldwide average oil/NGL and natural gas realizations, then describes commodity-price risks and estimated 2024 earnings sensitivities to oil and gas price changes, noting other factors that affect actual results. It explains refining-margin drivers, adverse market conditions, the value of financial strength, market-priced intersegment transactions, long-term supply-and-demand investment assumptions including greenhouse-gas costs, and regular review of nonstrategic assets for sale. Risk management covers diversification, commodity derivatives and trading, counterparty safeguards and controls, limited interest-rate and currency exposure, liquidity and commercial paper, and possible joint-venture funding constraints.

nodes.title: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES
key_items: Global Outlook and Cash Flow Assessment; Fair Value of Impaired Assets
Global Outlook and Cash Flow Assessment
Asset Retirement Obligations; Suspended Exploratory Well Costs
Pension Benefits; Litigation and Tax Contingencies
nodes.summary: The section explains critical accounting estimates and judgments underlying the Corporation’s integrated energy business and GAAP financial statements. It covers reserve estimation, definitions and revisions of proved and unproved reserves, and reserve-based depreciation; impairment monitoring, planning assumptions, cash-flow and fair-value methods, assessments of unproved, held-for-sale, and equity-method assets, recent impairment charges, and potential risks; asset retirement obligations; capitalization of suspended exploratory well costs; pension plans, funding, assumptions, returns, and expense sensitivity; and accounting, disclosure, and management review of litigation, other contingencies, and uncertain tax positions.

nodes.title: MANAGEMENT’S REPORT ON INTERNAL CONTROL OVER FINANCIAL REPORTING
key_items: Opinions on the Financial Statements and Internal Control over Financial Reporting; Basis for Opinions; Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
Opinions on the Financial Statements and Internal Control over Financial Reporting
Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
The Impact of Proved Developed Oil and Natural Gas Reserves on Upstream Property, Plant and Equipment, Net
nodes.summary: Management says Exxon Mobil’s financial-reporting controls were effective at December 31, 2023 under the COSO 2013 framework, excluding newly acquired Denbury (2% of assets and under 1% of revenues); executives signed the report. PwC’s audit found the consolidated financial statements fairly presented under U.S. GAAP and controls effective. The report explains audit responsibilities, procedures, reasonable assurance, control definitions and limitations, and Denbury’s exclusion. Its critical audit matter was how proved developed oil and gas reserves affect upstream PP&E and depreciation: auditors tested controls, reserve-estimation methods and assumptions, specialist qualifications, and production data and estimates. PwC has served since 1934.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENT OF INCOME
key_items: Net income (loss) including noncontrolling interests Other comprehensive income (loss) (net of income taxes)
nodes.summary: Presents ExxonMobil’s consolidated income and comprehensive income statements for 2023, 2022, and 2021, in millions of dollars. The income statement covers revenues and other income, operating costs and deductions, pretax income, income taxes, net income attributable to noncontrolling interests and ExxonMobil, and basic and diluted earnings per share. The comprehensive income statement reports net income, after-tax foreign-exchange and postretirement-benefit adjustments, total other comprehensive income, and comprehensive income attributable to noncontrolling interests and ExxonMobil. Notes are integral to the statements.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED BALANCE SHEET
key_items: Current assets; Total current assets; Total Assets
nodes.summary: Consolidated balance sheet for December 31, 2023 and 2022, in millions of dollars, listing current and noncurrent assets, total assets, current and long-term liabilities, and total liabilities. It also presents commitments and contingencies; equity components, including common stock, retained earnings, accumulated other comprehensive income, treasury stock, ExxonMobil’s share, and noncontrolling interests; and total equity and liabilities and equity. Notes to the consolidated financial statements are integral to the statements.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENT OF CASH FLOWS
key_items: CASH FLOWS FROM OPERATING ACTIVITIES; CASH FLOWS FROM INVESTING ACTIVITIES
nodes.summary: Presents ExxonMobil’s consolidated cash flows for 2021–2023, covering operating, investing, and financing activities, exchange-rate effects, and beginning and ending cash; includes a note on 2023 debt issued in connection with an entity sale. Shows changes in equity and common-share activity from 2020 through 2023, including earnings, dividends, other comprehensive income, repurchases, acquisitions, and dispositions. States that management is responsible for the consolidated statements, outlines the company’s businesses, and explains that U.S. GAAP reporting requires estimates whose actual results may differ.

Presents ExxonMobil’s 2021–2023 financial results, operating statistics, cash flows, capital employed, returns, structural cost savings, operating costs, segment earnings and adjustments, and capital and exploration spending. It discusses the business outlook, operating environment, strategies, taxes, environmental liabilities, market risks, liquidity, financing, and contingencies; explains non-GAAP measures and critical accounting estimates; and includes forward-looking-statement cautions, management’s and auditors’ internal-control reports, and consolidated income, balance-sheet, cash-flow, and equity statements.

Directs readers to the financial-section contents and exhibit index and notes there is no Form 10-K summary. Covers 2023–2022 segment and geographic business-profile results and operating measures, with definitions and rounding cautions. Presents 2021–2023 financial results, operating and cash-flow statistics, capital, returns, costs, segment earnings, and spending; discusses outlook, strategies, operating conditions, taxes, environmental liabilities, market risks, liquidity, financing, contingencies, non-GAAP measures, and accounting estimates; and includes management and auditor internal-control reports and consolidated financial statements.

summary: Reports gross and net developed and undeveloped acreage by region, subsidiary type, and year, with totals and Other Americas detail; explains property-specific rights, exploration assessments, relinquishments, extensions, and expected immaterial effects of scheduled expirations. It then describes country-specific petroleum license and contract terms across the Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia/Oceania, followed by global refining and chemical capacity and worldwide retail fuel-site counts. The section also covers legal proceedings, mine-safety applicability and executive officers; stock, dividends, repurchases, controls, and other Part II disclosures; proxy-related governance, compensation, ownership, and auditor matters in Part III; and Part IV financial, operating, risk, outlook, controls, and statement disclosures.

title: 1. Summary of Accounting Policies

nodes.title: Consolidation, Investments, and Revenue Recognition
key_items: Principles of Consolidation and Accounting for Investments
nodes.summary: Consolidated statements include controlled subsidiaries, qualifying variable-interest entities, and the Corporation’s share of certain upstream interests; significant influence is generally accounted for using the equity method, unless minority shareholders hold substantive participating rights. Equity-method investments are reviewed for impairment and written down to fair value when declines are other than temporary; related foreign currency adjustments enter accumulated other comprehensive income. Other equity securities are measured at fair value or, when fair value is not readily determinable, under a cost-based modified approach. Revenue is recognized when customers take control, with estimates for unavailable pricing indices later finalized; payments are generally due within 30 days. Unsatisfied delivery obligations are fulfilled through production or purchases and constrained by price volatility. Certain related inventory purchases and sales are recorded as book-value exchanges. Revenue, receivables, contract assets, and liabilities include items inside and outside ASC 606; long-term receivables are mainly outside its scope, while contract balances are mainly immaterial marketing assistance, prepayments, and volume discounts.

nodes.title: Income Taxes, Derivatives, Fair Value, and Inventories
nodes.summary: Explains the treatment of transaction taxes and global intangible low-taxed income taxes; derivative use, fair-value measurement, offsetting, and earnings or comprehensive-income recognition for nonhedges and fair-value or cash-flow hedges; the fair-value definition and three-level valuation-input hierarchy; and inventory valuation, included costs, excluded period expenses, and materials-and-supplies accounting.

nodes.title: Property, Plant, and Equipment
nodes.summary: The text describes accounting policies for property, plant, and equipment: successful-efforts cost capitalization and expensing, capitalized construction interest, and depreciation, depletion, and amortization methods and useful lives. It explains impairment indicators, monitoring, long-term price assumptions, and why standardized reserve cash-flow measures are not used for impairment decisions. It outlines the Global Outlook and Board-approved planning assumptions used to estimate undiscounted cash flows, including emissions costs and reserve volumes; fair-value measurement of impairments; and assessment of unproved properties, assets held for sale, and property-sale gains.

nodes.title: Environmental Liabilities and Currency Translation
nodes.summary: Environmental liabilities are recognized when obligations are probable and reasonably estimable; they are not offset by potential third-party recoveries, and projected cash expenditures are not discounted. Functional currencies for international subsidiaries reflect their primary economic environments: local currencies are used in Product Solutions and certain self-contained Upstream operations, while the U.S. dollar is used in high-inflation countries, Singapore, and some Upstream operations selling into dollar-denominated markets. Foreign-currency remeasurement gains and losses are included in income.

summary: Summarizes accounting policies for consolidation, investments, revenue and related balances; income and transaction taxes; derivatives, fair value and its valuation hierarchy; and inventory. Covers capitalization, depreciation and impairment of property and equipment, planning assumptions, reserves, unproved properties, held-for-sale assets and sale gains. Also addresses environmental liabilities and foreign-currency functional currencies, translation and remeasurement.

title: 2. Russia
summary: Following Russia’s military action in Ukraine, the Corporation announced plans in early 2022 to exit the Sakhalin-1 project. An impairment review found the asset group unrecoverable, producing first-quarter charges of $3.4 billion after tax ($4.6 billion before tax), mostly a full impairment. Russia terminated the Corporation’s interests on October 14, transferring operations to a Russian operator. Fourth-quarter results included a $1.1 billion after-tax benefit related largely to changed Sakhalin obligations, and the exit removed about 150 million oil-equivalent barrels from proved reserves at year-end.

title: 3. Miscellaneous Financial Information
summary: Notes disclose R&D expenses and foreign-exchange transaction losses for 2021–2023; LIFO inventory gains and the excess of replacement cost over carrying value; and year-end crude oil, petroleum, chemical, and gas/other inventories. They describe foreign-government fuel-price reimbursements, related receivables and accounting, expected program impacts, and nominally recorded emissions allowances. OCI tables report accumulated balances and annual changes by foreign-exchange and postretirement components, amounts reclassified to income, and related tax expenses or credits for 2021–2023.

title: Cash Flows and Working Capital
key_items: Cash interest paid; Total cash interest paid
summary: Explains cash and cash equivalents, 2023 Denbury acquisition and Esso Thailand sale, and asset-sale gains and losses for 2021–2023. Reports income taxes and cash interest paid, including capitalized interest. Presents 2023 and 2022 receivables, notes and loans payable, and accounts payable and accrued liabilities. Describes receivable scope and customer credit characteristics, and notes that $0.3 billion of committed credit lines were unused at year-end 2023.

title: 7. Equity Company Information
key_items: Upstream; Energy Products, Chemical Products, and/or Specialty Products
Energy Products, Chemical Products, and/or Specialty Products
summary: Note 7 describes equity companies, their industries and regions, sales to ExxonMobil affiliates (9%, 11%, and 10% in 2023–2021), investment accounting, and upstream impairments of $0.6 billion, $0.6 billion, and $0.2 billion. It presents 2023–2021 summarized financial results and assets, liabilities, and net assets for total equity companies and ExxonMobil’s share, plus significant companies and ownership percentages by business segment. Note 8 reports 2023 and 2022 equity-method investments and advances, other investments, and long-term receivables, totaling $49.8 billion and $47.6 billion, respectively.

title: 9. Property, Plant and Equipment and Asset Retirement Obligations
summary: The note reports property, plant and equipment cost and net balances by business for 2023 and 2022. It details impairment charges: $3.3 billion in 2023, mainly for idled Santa Ynez assets, $4.5 billion in 2022, primarily related to exiting Sakhalin-1, and $1.2 billion in 2021; charges are mainly recorded in depreciation/depletion and exploration expenses. Accumulated depreciation and depletion was $272.445 billion in 2023 and $268.001 billion in 2022. It explains how asset retirement obligations are estimated, recorded, capitalized, depreciated, and accreted, including conditional Product Solutions obligations whose settlement dates cannot be estimated. A rollforward shows obligations rising to $12.989 billion in 2023; long-term amounts were $11.942 billion and $9.650 billion in 2023 and 2022, with estimated payments of $1.047 billion in 2024 and $899 million in 2025.

title: 10. Accounting for Suspended Exploratory Well Costs
summary: The note explains when exploratory well costs remain capitalized: sufficient reserves must be found and assessment of reserves and project viability must be progressing. It presents 2021–2023 balances, additions, expenses, reclassifications, divestments and other changes, equity-company amounts, and cost aging. It also reports project counts by cost age. Of 31 projects with costs capitalized over a year in 2023, 16 had recent or planned activity and 15 completed exploration but were progressing toward development; their country, project, costs, drilling dates and development status are listed, totaling $2.389 billion.

title: 11. Leases
key_items: Lease Cost; Balance Sheet; Right of use assets
Total lease payments; Total lease liability; Other Information; Noncash right of use assets recorded for lease liabilities
Noncash right of use assets recorded for lease liabilities
summary: Notes 11–12 describe lease accounting, with right-of-use assets and liabilities recognized for leases over one year; leases are mostly operating, with limited finance leases. They report lease costs, balance-sheet assets and liabilities, terms and discount rates, payment maturities, future commitments for leases not yet commenced, and related cash flows and noncash additions. The notes also present 2021–2023 net income attributable to ExxonMobil, weighted-average shares, earnings per share, and dividends per share, including share-count and dilution clarifications.

title: 13. Financial Instruments and Derivatives
summary: The note reports 2023 and 2022 fair values and hierarchy levels for derivative assets and liabilities, equity-company balances, other financial assets and liabilities, and long-term debt, including netting, collateral effects, carrying-value differences, and balance-sheet classifications. Equity-company balances and acquisition-related contingent consideration use Level 3 valuation inputs. Unoffset collateral under master netting arrangements was $800 million in 2023 and $1,494 million in 2022. It describes derivative risk management, trading presentation and lack of hedge accounting for commodity derivatives, immaterial currency and interest-rate derivatives, and controls mitigating counterparty credit risk. It also provides 2023/2022 commodity derivative net positions and derivative gains or losses by income-statement line for 2023–2021.

title: 14. Long-Term Debt
summary: At year-end 2023, long-term debt was $37.483 billion, including $32.510 billion payable in U.S. dollars and $4.973 billion in foreign currencies; $4.009 billion due within one year was classified as current. Debt redeemed and extinguished in 2022 is noted. The text gives debt maturities for 2025–2028, $1.3 billion of unused credit lines, and a perfectly effective €5.0 billion net-investment hedge. A 2023/2022 debt table details issuers, notes, rates, maturities, balances, finance leases, bonds, issuance costs, and premiums.

title: 15. Incentive Program
summary: The 2003 Incentive Program authorizes stock options, SARs, restricted stock, and other awards for eligible employees and qualifying affiliates. Options and SARs are granted at no less than market value and have maximum 10-year terms; the plan permits 220 million shares, has no fixed end date, and had 54 million shares available at year-end 2023. The text describes restricted-award eligibility, forfeiture and transfer restrictions, grant amounts, treasury-stock issuance, cash-settlement accounting, and vesting schedules. It reports 2023 award activity and grant-date values, grant prices and values for 2021–2023, unrecognized compensation cost and recognition period, compensation expense and tax benefits, vested award fair values, and cash settlement payments.

title: 16. Litigation and Other Contingencies
summary: Note 16 explains ExxonMobil’s litigation contingency accounting and disclosures, including climate-change and Louisiana coastal-erosion lawsuits, its view that the claims lack merit, and its assessment that material adverse outcomes are remote. It also reports guarantees and other contingent obligations and long-term commitments. Note 17 presents pension and postretirement benefit assumptions, obligations, assets, costs, funded status and balance-sheet/OCI effects; funding and investment policies; 2022–23 fair-value hierarchies; plans with obligations exceeding assets; and expected 2024 contributions, benefit payments, and Medicare subsidy receipts.

title: 18. Disclosures about Segments and Related Information
summary: The disclosure identifies four reportable segments—Upstream, Energy Products, Chemical Products, and Specialty Products—based on the nature of their operations, and lists each segment’s activities and product categories. It notes that after-tax earnings include transfers at estimated market prices; Corporate and Financing interest revenue comes from cash deposits and marketable securities, and non-debt-related interest expense was $234 million in 2023, $117 million in 2022, and $103 million in 2021. Tables provide 2021–2023 segment and geographic financial data, including earnings, revenues, expenses, taxes, capital additions, equity investments, and assets; figures may not sum precisely due to rounding.

title: Revenue from Contracts with Customers
summary: The notes explain that sales and other operating revenue includes revenue both within and outside ASC 606. Revenue outside ASC 606 primarily comes from physically settled commodity contracts accounted for as derivatives. Contract terms, credit quality, and customer types are generally similar across both categories. A table presents 2023, 2022, and 2021 revenue from customer contracts, revenue outside ASC 606, and totals, in millions of dollars; figures are not shown in the text.

title: Geographic
summary: The text reports ExxonMobil’s geographic sales and operating revenue and long-lived assets for 2021–2023, including U.S./non-U.S. totals and major non-U.S. countries, with attribution caveats. It details income tax expense and other taxes by U.S. and non-U.S. operations for each year, deferred-tax effects of tax-law changes, and the EU energy-sector excess-profits tax and its charges. It also reconciles reported tax expense to the 21% theoretical U.S. rate, including equity-method, foreign, state, and other effects, and gives effective tax rates.

title: Total
summary: The notes reconcile 2021–2023 income tax expense and effective tax rates to the 21% U.S. statutory rate, including equity-method, foreign, state, and other effects; 2022 and 2023 figures include specified European energy-sector taxes. They detail deferred tax assets, liabilities, valuation allowances, balance-sheet classification, and the treatment of indefinitely reinvested foreign earnings. The notes also explain uncertain-tax-position recognition and annual balance changes, potential effects and resolution uncertainty, IRS issues, possible 12-month balance changes, open examination years by jurisdiction, and tax-related interest and penalties.

title: 20. Divestment Activities
summary: In 2023, divestments generated about $4.1 billion in proceeds and $0.6 billion in net after-tax earnings, including sales of Aera Energy, Esso Thailand, the Billings Refinery, U.S. unconventional assets, and smaller assets. In 2022, they generated about $5.2 billion and $0.4 billion, including Romanian unproved assets and Canadian and U.S. unconventional assets. The planned sale of Mobil Producing Nigeria remained subject to approvals and legal proceedings, with closing and any loss dependent on their resolution. The Santa Ynez Unit sale closed February 14, 2024, with no material first-quarter financial impact expected.

title: 21. Mergers and Acquisitions

title: EXXON MOBIL CORPORATION SHORT TERM INCENTIVE PROGRAM

nodes.title: I. Purposes
nodes.summary:
EXXON MOBIL CORPORATION SHORT TERM INCENTIVE PROGRAM
(as amended October 23, 2023)
I. Purposes
The Short Term Incentive Program is intended to help reward, retain, and motivate selected employees of the Corporation and its affiliates by recognizing efforts and accomplishments which contribute materially to the success of the Corporation's business interests.

nodes.title: II. Definitions
nodes.summary: Defines the Program’s governing terms: administrative and granting authorities; affiliates, awards, bonuses, bonus units, and earnings bonus units; the Board, Compensation Committee, Corporation, employees, grantees, and beneficiaries; detrimental activity and its misconduct, breach, and conflict-of-interest grounds; Exchange Act, Section 16, reporting persons, and basic earnings per share; the Program and calendar year; and resignation, standard retirement time, and termination, including relevant timing and employment-transfer rules.

nodes.title: III. Administration
nodes.summary: The Board is the Program’s ultimate administrative authority and may interpret and administer its provisions, delegating authority to a committee (which need not be a Board committee, except for the Compensation Committee). Subject to the Board or authorized committee, the Chairman and delegates establish operating requirements and procedures, make final determinations and interpretations on outstanding awards, and exercise other assigned administrative powers.

nodes.title: Award Securities, Ceilings, Authority, and Eligibility
key_items: VI. Right to Grant Awards; Reserved Powers; Eligibility
nodes.summary: Awards are not payable in corporate equity securities and are intended to fall outside Section 16; reporting-person awards may be amended or annulled if deemed equity securities. The Compensation Committee sets and may revise an annual ceiling covering bonuses and bonus units’ maximum settlement value. The Board selects participants and controls award decisions, with specified delegation options. Eligible recipients must be current or recent employees of the Corporation or qualifying affiliates; awards are discretionary, confer no future entitlement, and may not go to Compensation Committee members.

nodes.title: Bonus Program Terms and Settlement
key_items: X. Deferred and Installment Settlement; Interest Equivalents
nodes.summary: The Program continues until the Board terminates it. Bonuses may be paid in cash, bonus units, or both; each grant sets settlement timing and method, including regular and potentially accelerated settlement dates for bonus units. Settlement may be deferred or made in installments, but no later than ten years after termination. Deferred cash awards may earn interest equivalents, paid currently or compounded and settled with the award, subject to the same forfeiture conditions. Interest credits are not new grants and do not count toward the Compensation Committee’s award ceiling.

nodes.title: XI. Termination; Detrimental Activity
nodes.summary: Before standard retirement, termination other than death generally forfeits all unpaid or unsettled awards unless the administrative authority allows otherwise; for reporting persons, this is the Compensation Committee. The authority may set termination as the date of resignation notice, acceptance of another job, expressed intent to resign, or discharge—not necessarily the last payroll day. If a grantee engages in detrimental activity, awards may be canceled even after employment ends. Awards may also be suspended during investigation of suspected detrimental activity or indications of a move to another employer or intent to resign.

nodes.title: XII. Material Negative Restatement
nodes.summary: The document addresses recovery of awards following negative restatements: covered executives are subject to the Corporation’s Rule 10D-1 policy, and the Compensation Committee may seek additional recovery from grantees who were reporting persons when awards were paid or granted, within five years of payment, excluding amounts recoverable under that policy. These obligations do not depend on personal involvement and supplement other remedies. At a grantee’s death, rights and obligations pass to a designated beneficiary or, absent one, the estate representative or heirs; the administrative authority sets designation procedures and may alter deferred-award settlement. The Board may amend the Program, generally affecting outstanding awards automatically, and the granting authority may amend awards subject to applicable terms. The Corporation may withhold cash to meet award-related tax and contribution obligations.

nodes.title: Awards: Recovery, Death, Amendments, and Taxes
key_items: XIV. Amendments to this Program and Outstanding Awards
nodes.summary: Reporting persons’ payment obligations for recoveries are independent of involvement in the events causing a restatement, and do not limit other remedies against responsible parties. At a grantee’s death, rights and obligations pass to the designated beneficiary or, absent one, the estate representative or lawful heirs; designations must follow established procedures, and deferred-award settlement may be changed or accelerated unless the award instrument says otherwise. The Board may amend the Program, generally effective immediately for outstanding awards; the granting authority may also amend outstanding awards within Program requirements. The Corporation may withhold cash to meet award-related tax and contribution obligations.

nodes.title: XVI. Non-US Awards
nodes.summary:
XVI. Non-US Awards
Subject to the limitations contained in this Program, the granting authority may establish different terms and conditions for awards to persons who are residents or nationals of countries other than the United States in order to accommodate the local laws, tax policies, or customs of such countries. The granting authority may adopt one or more supplements or sub-plans under this Program to implement those different terms and conditions.

nodes.title: XVII. General Provisions
nodes.summary: Awards are nontransferable except by inheritance and are protected from attachment, though beneficiary designation is not a transfer. Award types and terms may vary by grantee, and awards may be issued for no, minimum legally required, or other authorized consideration. The administrative authority determines how awards are documented, with its records controlling disputes. Awards do not create employment contracts or restrict termination. Grantees have only unsecured contractual rights to settlement amounts. New York and U.S. law govern, excluding conflict-of-law rules.

key_items: Exxon Mobil Corporation Rule 10D-1 Recoupment Policy Effective December 1, 2023
nodes.summary: Effective December 1, 2023, the policy implements NYSE Rule 10D-1 alongside other available recovery remedies, preventing duplicate recovery. It requires prompt recoupment of excess compensation received by covered executives during the recovery period after a financial restatement, without regard to taxes. The committee reasonably estimates stock-price or shareholder-return effects and documents estimates for the NYSE. Recovery may be impracticable if documented enforcement expenses exceed the amount or recovery threatens certain tax-qualified retirement plans. Recovery methods include repayment, set-off, cancellation, or reducing future compensation. The corporation will not insure or indemnify executives for losses; the Compensation Committee administers the policy, with final, binding determinations.
